source.title: Probing the Impact of Scale on Data-Efficient, Generalist Transformer World Models for Atari

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper and appendices; no truncation or garbling apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how transformer world-model capacity affects validation fidelity under fixed offline Atari data, using depth sweeps and a unified-training comparison rather than the claim versions’ specified experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports depth-scaling outcomes for world-model training and validation loss, including task-specific trends and unified-model results. These are not random-label memorization tests, width sweeps on the specified networks, image-classifier architecture comparisons, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout interventions, sharpness measurements, or memorized-example removals.
record.test_reason: The study measures transformer world-model validation loss as capacity changes chiefly through depth. V2 specifically concerns widening beyond the width needed to fit the training data. The unified experiment varies width among underparameterized configurations, then varies depth at fixed width among configurations reaching near-zero training loss. Neither experiment establishes the post-interpolation width effect. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: individual scaling trends depend on the environment, while unified training stabilizes validation performance as capacity increases. The authors also report that appropriate individual-model scaling improves downstream policy performance. Their explanation that task diversity regularizes scaling remains an interpretation; the main unified experiment increases total data volume, and the fixed-budget appendix provides only preliminary evidence from two environment pairs.
record.recipe_differences: Transformer world models trained on fixed offline Atari trajectories; capacity varied by depth and, for unified configurations, depth and embedding dimension. The measures are world-model training and validation losses, not the claim versions’ specified test-error experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling outcomes vary by environment and by individual versus unified training; unified training stabilizes the trend. The study reports eight independent runs for individual curves and four runs for the fixed-budget appendix ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Individual transformer world models exhibit degradation, monotonic improvement, saturation, or double descent as depth increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With fixed offline Atari data, the relationship between transformer depth and validation loss depends on the environment.

fits_no_version.finding: Among unified configurations reaching near-zero training loss, increasing depth at embedding dimension 2048 improves or sustains validation performance across 26 environments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint training across Atari environments can stabilize validation-loss scaling with transformer depth.

record.problems: The evidence concerns Atari world-model validation fidelity and varies capacity chiefly through depth, so it does not directly establish behavior for the claim versions’ specified architectures, test-error measures, or interventions. Several results are described qualitatively without numerical loss values in the supplied text; unified environment-wise figures are not numerically tabulated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted. Appendix I describes a fixed-budget 100k-frame ablation for Amidar mixed with Assault or Gopher, but its results are shown in Figure 15 without textual numerical values; the figure description reports that mixing with Assault delays the overfitting spike more than mixing with Gopher. This bears on the same capacity-generalization relationship but is not separately extracted because its exact condition-specific outcome is figure-only and the 60-row limit is not binding.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the matched natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy comparison.
Held-out performance when width increases beyond the width needed to fit training data. The study instead chiefly varies depth and uses AdamW with weight decay 0.1 and early stopping.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size interventions under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on data size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparison with other measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The authors' interpolation-threshold interpretation should be distinguished from the measured loss trends: they describe Amidar as not surpassing that threshold despite reporting effectively zero training loss for L ≥ 4. This ambiguity does not turn the depth sweep into a test of V2.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of held-out natural-label accuracy.
Uses transformer depth rather than width; Atari world models rather than one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10; reports validation loss rather than test error.
No convolutional versus fully connected world-model comparison.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: individual transformer world model (Amidar)
rows.size_stated: Embedding dimension 512; depth L ∈ {2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 96}; approximately 6 million to 300 million parameters across sweep.
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer depth with fixed embedding dimension and evaluated training and validation loss.
rows.measure: Validation loss as a measure of world-model fidelity/generalization
rows.value: L = 8 to L = 12 achieve the lowest validation loss; increasing depth to L = 24, 48, and 96 degrades fidelity. Training loss effectively reaches zero for L ≥ 4.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars represent one standard error.
rows.note: The paper describes this as remaining in the classical overfitting regime; precise loss values are not stated in the supplied text.
rows.check: The reported degradation concerns increased depth at fixed embedding dimension, so it cannot establish a reversal of V2's width effect. The qualitative loss summary matches the text.

rows.subject: individual transformer world model (Assault)
rows.size_stated: Embedding dimension 512; depth L ∈ {2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 96}; approximately 6 million to 300 million parameters across sweep.
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer depth with fixed embedding dimension and evaluated training and validation loss.
rows.measure: Validation loss as a measure of world-model fidelity/generalization
rows.value: Validation performance improves monotonically as model depth increases.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars represent one standard error.
rows.note: The paper characterizes this task as already beyond the interpolation threshold at the smallest swept sizes.
rows.check: Monotonic improvement with depth does not measure improvement from widening beyond the width needed to fit. The qualitative result matches the text.

rows.subject: individual transformer world model (Freeway)
rows.size_stated: Embedding dimension 512; depth L ∈ {2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 96}; approximately 6 million to 300 million parameters across sweep.
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer depth with fixed embedding dimension and evaluated training and validation loss.
rows.measure: Validation loss as a measure of world-model fidelity/generalization
rows.value: Curves for L = 8 through L = 96 essentially overlap, with no significant gain over the smaller models; saturation at L = 4 is reported.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars represent one standard error.
rows.note: The authors describe additional scaling as redundant though not harmful.
rows.check: Saturation under a depth sweep cannot establish absence of V2's width effect. The reported overlap and lack of significant gain match the text.

rows.subject: individual transformer world model (Pong)
rows.size_stated: Embedding dimension 512; depth L ∈ {2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 96}; approximately 6 million to 300 million parameters across sweep.
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer depth with fixed embedding dimension and evaluated training and validation loss.
rows.measure: Validation loss as a measure of world-model fidelity/generalization
rows.value: Validation loss improves from L = 2 to L = 8, deteriorates from L = 12 to L = 48, then declines at L = 96, surpassing the classical best at L = 8.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars represent one standard error.
rows.note: The authors characterize this trajectory as canonical double descent.
rows.check: The depth-based double-descent trajectory measures a different capacity intervention from V2. It cannot be classified as partial evidence for continued improvement with width.

rows.subject: unified transformer world model Wuni
rows.size_stated: Underparameterized: L = 8, d ∈ {512, 1024}; overparameterized: L ∈ {4, 8, 24}, d = 2048; largest configuration approximately 1.2 billion parameters.
rows.stage_stated: trained on aggregated fixed offline data from 26 Atari environments
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss across five capacity configurations in unified training.

conditions.value: all 26 Atari games; environment-wise curves shown for seven representative games in Figure 5, full results in Appendix G

rows.measure: Validation loss as a measure of world-model fidelity/generalization
rows.baseline: Underparameterized configurations; precise values not stated.
rows.value: After entering the overparameterized regime, larger models improve or sustain performance across environments; the paper reports no rank reversals or inverted-U curves.
rows.locator: Sections 4.3 and Appendix G; Figures 5 and 13
rows.note: The paper reports the overall result across all environments; precise per-environment values are not stated.
rows.check: The configurations reaching near-zero training loss all have embedding dimension 2048 and differ in depth. Smaller-width configurations remain underparameterized. This does not test widening past the width needed to fit; the aggregate row also combines improvement and saturation.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Individual Atari world models under the tested depth sweep
reader_labels.reason: Capacity scaling varied by environment: it worsened validation loss in Amidar, improved it in Assault, saturated in Freeway, and showed double descent in Pong (R1–R4). These experiments use depth and world-model fidelity, so they qualify the scaling pattern in this setting rather than directly testing the version’s specified width and test-error setup.
